Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following
revelations he had two affairs
, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis for
one of the world's most valuable firms
- a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.
Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".
Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants,
according to the Financial Times
,
external
, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang
since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

New rules
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.
The move comes ahead of a
meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping
, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.
The interim rules
will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.
The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.
He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".
In 2025, Nvidia won
an approval to sell some advanced AI chips
in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of
scrutiny over deals abroad
.
The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.
Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.
But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.
But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to  companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry.
US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including
before the House Select Committee on China
to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
'A handshake with Jensen'
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,"
he posted on X.
,
external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was
reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023,
said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer
Colette Kress is leading the firm
and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".
Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.
The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including
a massive Microsoft outage
, a network failure that
grounded all US flights
, and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".
Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.
Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.

Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".
The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.
The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.
Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.
Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.
US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.
Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.
Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.
As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.
Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".
That issue resolved within a few hours.
The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.
The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.
The United issue is separate from
the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)
, but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.
On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.
The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.
They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.
Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.
"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.
With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.
That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.
'We've saved thousands'
They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.
In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.
The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.
Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".
Image source,
Elizabeth Wilcox
Image caption,
Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get along
While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.
Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.
It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.
It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".
"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."
Image source,
Elizabeth Wilcox
Image caption,
The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver home
Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.
While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.
"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.
Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.
'We have house meetings'
Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.
While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.
She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."
They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.
"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.
Image source,
Sabrina Bowman
Image caption,
Sabrina Bowman says it is important to have open communication
In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.
For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.
Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.
Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.
"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

SPEECH
The science and practice of monetary policy communication: the ECB experience
Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Bank of England and its Watchers Conference
London, 10 November 2026
Monetary policy is about more than just the latest interest rate decision. It also involves communication about future economic developments and the factors shaping future policy decisions.
[
1
]
By steering the expectations of financial market participants, central bank communication shapes the full set of financial market prices across the maturity and risk spectrums, in turn affecting financing conditions and decisions around credit, saving and investment. The decisions of households and firms are also affected by their beliefs about monetary policy, which depend on how the central bank communicates.
[
2
]
I will divide this speech into two parts. In the first part, I will review recent contributions by ECB staff on the science of monetary policy communication.
[
3
]
In the second part, I will discuss the practice of monetary policy communication from an ECB perspective.
The science of monetary policy communication
Greater data availability, increased computing power and artificial intelligence have substantially expanded the tools available for analysing central bank communication. Until recently, researchers relied on dictionary-based approaches to quantify the content and tone of monetary policy statements and speeches. This involved categorising specific words and expressions associated with a restrictive or accommodative stance, or with different assessments of inflation and the economic outlook.
[
4
]
Machine learning techniques and large language models (LLMs) now allow for the extensive analysis of large volumes of text in a more automated manner, taking into account the context in which words are used instead of relying solely on the frequency of individual words or predefined expressions.
[
5
]
Recent ECB research illustrates these possibilities. A set of novel, LLM-based in-house measures of the tone of ECB monetary policy communication confirms that it becomes more hawkish during tightening phases and more dovish during easing periods. These shifts in communication closely track developments in the deposit facility rate (Chart 1, panel a).
[
6
]
The importance of communication is also illustrated by the research finding that information extracted from ECB monetary policy statements can improve forecasts of euro area core inflation several quarters ahead, even when controlling for the contributions of Eurosystem and ECB staff projections.
[
7
]
These indicators can also be employed to test whether central bank communication follows systematic patterns that reflect the economic outlook and the policy stance. Indeed, the evidence suggests that central banks tend to communicate in a systematic manner, following “communication rules”.
[
8
]
By estimating a systematic relationship between the tone of communication on monetary policy, economic activity and inflation, ECB staff find that, in line with our primary objective of price stability, ECB communication on monetary policy systematically places more emphasis on inflation developments (Chart 1, panel b).
These new tools therefore provide valuable insights into aspects of communication that conventional financial market indicators may not fully capture. At the same time, their use requires careful validation, since the results depend on how questions are formulated and what data are used for training.

]

Financial markets
Financial market participants closely follow central bank communication because it provides information about both the economic and inflation outlook and the expected path of monetary policy. Both of these dimensions are relevant for asset pricing and investment decisions.
Central bank communication can influence interest rate expectations and financial conditions, independently from actual policy changes.
[
10
]
Research shows that financial analysts reassess the monetary policy stance following ECB Governing Council announcements, considering both the policy decision and the accompanying communication. Unexpected revisions in their assessment contain information beyond conventional market-based monetary policy surprises and are associated with significant effects on economic and financial conditions. For instance, even when an interest rate decision is widely anticipated and generates little immediate market reaction, the accompanying communication may lead market analysts to reassess how restrictive is monetary policy or how it is likely to evolve.

The importance of communication extends beyond Governing Council meetings. Research examining thousands of speeches, interviews, hearings and other events shows that communication in the time period between meetings can affect market interest rates across maturities. It can help markets anticipate policy changes, particularly ahead of tightening episodes, and its cumulative effect over time can be comparable to that of policy announcements, especially at longer maturities (Chart 2).

Beyond shaping expectations about the future path of policy rates, communication also affects financial conditions more broadly. The tone of ECB communication can influence monetary policy uncertainty and premia on risky assets.

]
In particular, financial markets respond to several dimensions of monetary policy news: the current policy rate, the expected path of rates, and market and sovereign risk (“target”, “path”, and “risk” in Chart 3, respectively).

Households and firms
Communicating with households and firms presents different challenges to communicating with markets. Unlike professional market participants, most households do not closely follow central bank communication. And even when they do encounter central bank messages, they may interpret their implications differently to market analysts. Research presented in our 2021 monetary policy strategy review suggests that information about the new inflation target reached only around one in ten consumers in the months following its announcement. Most learned about the new inflation target through television, radio and newspapers rather than directly from the ECB (Chart 4).

Reaching households, however, is just one part of the process. Attention to inflation varies with the economic environment. When inflation is high, households and firms tend to pay more attention, while they pay less attention when inflation is low and stable (Chart 5).
[
15
]
This matters for the transmission of monetary policy. What households and firms believe about future inflation, and how confident they are that the central bank will deliver price stability, shapes how they set wages and prices and how they adjust their spending and saving when we change interest rates.
[
16
]
When inflation is high, households tend to be more attentive, but they may also be less responsive to information they already know. This underscores the importance of tailoring communication to the economic environment to ensure that messages reach households when inflation is low while providing clear, relevant and informative explanations when inflation becomes more salient.
[
17
]
Households typically interpret monetary policy in terms of how it directly affects their economic circumstances. Euro area consumers tend to associate monetary policy primarily with borrowing costs rather than directly with inflation. Those who emphasise the borrowing-cost channel may also respond more strongly to a rate rise in their planned spending decisions.
[
18
]
The expectations of firms are also important for monetary policy transmission. Their views about future inflation influence pricing, wage-setting and investment decisions, and ultimately the evolution of inflation itself. Recent evidence shows that attention paid by firms to inflation varies considerably over time, increasing when inflationary pressures become more pronounced (Chart 5, panel b).

Macroeconomic impact of monetary policy communication
Unexpected shifts in monetary policy communication (“communication shocks”) can influence activity and inflation. Relative to the impact of those of unexpected interest rate decisions (“interest rate shocks”), the effects of “communication shocks” tend to be smaller and slower to materialise but can nevertheless be significant (Chart 6).

It is also important to recognise that monetary policy announcements convey different types of information. Markets respond not only to the decision, but also to what it reveals about the assessment of the economy. A surprise rate rise may signal tighter policy, but it may also lead markets to reassess the strength of activity or the persistence of inflation. Research has developed methods to separate policy surprises from the so-called central bank information effects, and more recently from surprises about how the central bank responds to publicly available news. These distinctions are important in order to assess accurately the effects of monetary policy communication.
[
20
]
Recent research shows that these channels are distinct and can be identified together, which sharpens estimates of how policy affects the economy.
[
21
]
For the ECB, research finds that estimated monetary policy surprises on meeting days – the movements in interest rates in a narrow window around the announcement – are partially inferable from euro area equity market changes over the six weeks preceding the meeting.
[
22
]
Market reactions to speeches, by contrast, show no such pattern.
[
23
]
Information conveyed by ECB announcements also travels across borders. The evidence suggests that it accounts for an important part of the co-movement of German and US government bond yields around ECB announcement days.
[
24
]
ECB staff have also analysed the implications of uncertainty for monetary policy communication. When economic conditions are changing rapidly, it may be preferable to place greater emphasis on the current state of the economy than on precise indications about the distant future.
[
25
]
The appropriate degree of precision also depends on how confident policymakers are in their forecasts and how that confidence is perceived.
[
26
]
Moreover, how policymakers express confidence in their assessment – or acknowledge developments that differ from expectations – can itself be informative about the policy stance.

Trust and credibility
Finally, economic agents need to not only clearly understand central bank messages but also trust that the words will be followed by action. Explaining why the ECB’s inflation target matters for economic stability can strengthen public confidence in our commitment to keep prices stable. Such explanations are particularly effective among people with lower financial literacy, as they can help them understand how monetary policy contributes to achieving the inflation target. The effects can persist for several months but tend to fade over time.
[
28
]
Building and maintaining credibility therefore requires more than communicating individual decisions clearly. It requires explaining, consistently and repeatedly, why our objective matters and how our policies contribute to achieving it.
[

The practice of monetary policy communication
Having reviewed recent scientific research on monetary policy communication in the first part of this speech, I will now turn to a discussion of monetary policy communication in practice.
Throughout its history, the ECB has adapted its communication content to changes in the economy, the instruments activated in setting the monetary policy stance and the nature of the uncertainty facing policymakers (Chart 7).

Before the global financial crisis, ECB monetary policy communication focused on explaining decisions and making the underlying reaction function more predictable, without explicitly signalling an interest rate path.
[
30
]
Since its inception, the ECB has held press conferences to accompany its policy decisions. The publication of staff macroeconomic projections from 2004 onwards provided further information about the outlook. Policy decisions were systematically related to the assessment of risks surrounding the projected inflation path, while communication between meetings could help markets anticipate turning points. For instance, the speech by ECB President Trichet on 18 November 2005 ahead of the December 2005 interest rate increase helped prepare markets for the first interest rate increase in five years.
[
31
]
Through these steps, news about the orientation of monetary policy influenced medium- and longer-term yields even before the era of explicit forward guidance.
[
32
]
The global financial crisis and the euro area sovereign debt crisis fundamentally changed the environment. Amid severe financial stress, effective communication played an essential role in restoring confidence and supporting smooth monetary policy transmission. This was particularly evident in the summer of 2012 due to rising financial fragmentation and elevated sovereign risk premia. The ECB's commitment to do “whatever it takes” to preserve the euro, followed by the announcement of the Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT) instrument, helped alleviate these concerns and contributed to a substantial decline in sovereign bond yields and narrowing spreads in the countries most affected by the crisis. This episode illustrates how communication backed by a clear policy commitment can safeguard smooth monetary policy transmission.
[
33
]
As policy rates approached the effective lower bound, influencing expectations about future rates became all the more important. The ECB introduced explicit rate forward guidance in July 2013. By communicating on the future policy path, rate forward guidance sought to influence market expectations and financing conditions beyond the immediate policy horizon. Experience showed that design matters. Longer-horizon and state-contingent guidance can reduce uncertainty about future rates by clarifying the conditions under which policy may change.
By contrast, short-horizon or open-ended guidance may be less effective and can even increase uncertainty if it leaves markets unsure about the central bank's future course of action.
[
34
]
The interaction with other instruments matters as well. Asset purchases can reinforce the effectiveness of forward guidance, while clear information about the scale of purchase programmes can reduce uncertainty. However, linking the sequencing of asset purchases to interest rate decisions can also constrain policy flexibility when economic conditions change unexpectedly.
As a result of the 2021 monetary policy strategy review, the Governing Council adopted the symmetric two per cent inflation target. At the following monetary policy meeting (July 2021), it revised its rate forward guidance by linking the expected policy path more explicitly to the inflation outlook and realised progress in underlying inflation. This reinforced the commitment to a forceful or persistent monetary policy response aimed at achieving the inflation target when inflation appeared at risk of undershooting the target.
[
35
]
[
36
]
However, in the wake of the 2021-2022 inflation surge, the guidance that had been designed specifically for an environment of persistently below-target inflation was no longer appropriate. The period between July 2022 and March 2023 constituted an important transition phase. In July 2022 the Governing Council moved away from the effective lower bound by raising the policy rate from minus 50 basis points to zero.
[
37
]
In line with the 2021 strategy decision that the ECB key interest rates are the primary monetary policy instrument away from the effective lower bound, the monetary policy statement did not provide specific guidance on the expected future rate path. However, it did provide directional guidance, indicating that further rate normalisation would be appropriate at upcoming meetings, even if the exact calibration would be data-dependent and decided on a meeting-by-meeting basis. The following four meetings (September 2022 to February 2023) maintained directional guidance, with a pair of 75 basis point hikes followed by a pair of 50 basis point hikes.
In addition, the February 2023 meeting articulated the intention to also hike by 50 basis points at the March meeting, which was subsequently implemented. However, having quickly raised the policy rate from -50 to 300 between July 2022 and March 2023, the March 2023 monetary policy statement replaced directional guidance with the reaction function guidance that future interest rate decisions would be based on the inflation outlook in light of incoming economic and financial data, underlying inflation dynamics and the strength of monetary policy transmission. These criteria would be assessed on a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting basis. These elements of the reaction function remain in place. An explicit role for the risks surrounding the inflation outlook was added in July 2025: this reflected one implementation of the conclusion of the 2025 monetary policy strategy assessment that monetary policy decisions should explicitly incorporate this risk assessment.
Although it turned out that the following four meetings would also deliver hikes (25 basis points at each meeting, bringing the policy rate to 400 basis points), there was a clear gear shift at the March 2023 meeting. In essence, after a series of rapid and outsized hikes, the gap between the policy rate and the plausible range of the “appropriate level” of the policy rate was no longer so wide as to justify ongoing formal directional guidance.
[
38
]
While formal directional guidance may be appropriate in the early phases of a forceful monetary policy response to a large inflation shock in either direction, it may convey an excessive level of certainty about the future rate path in the later phases (after a large adjustment has already been put in place). Similarly, avoiding formal directional guidance is prudent in implementing a measured monetary policy response to less extreme inflation shocks.
[
39
]
The framework guidance provided by the Governing Council can be interpreted as implementing the strategic approach to making monetary policy decisions that was laid out in the 2021 monetary policy strategy statement.
[
40
]
In particular, the 2021 strategy committed to basing monetary policy decisions on an integrated assessment of all relevant factors, taking into account the interdependencies between the economic analysis of real and nominal variables and the monetary and financial analysis that focused on the monetary transmission mechanism.
Since it would be unwise to rely exclusively on inflation projections, especially during times of high uncertainty, a balanced approach that takes into account both the forward-looking inflation outlook and the information revealed by the realised path of underlying inflation is preferable, with underlying inflation indicators distilling the realised inflation data to uncover the components most relevant for the medium term. In calibrating monetary policy, it is also essential to rely on the latest assessment of the strength of monetary transmission, given the range of uncertainty about the timing and strength of the macro-financial impact of shifts in the monetary policy stance and the scope for exogenous shocks to financial conditions and financing conditions.
[
41
]
Framework guidance delivers a systematic approach to monetary policy that is interpretable by financial market participants and external experts. The 2021 monetary policy strategy statement highlighted that monetary policy decisions are communicated through the monetary policy statement, the press conference, the Economic Bulletin and the monetary policy accounts. Together with the publication of the quarterly staff macroeconomic projections exercises, these releases provide the analytical underpinnings of how the reaction function criteria are assessed. Further analysis is provided through staff working papers and contributions to the ECB Blog, along with presentations and speeches by ECB Executive Board members.
[
42
]
Recent ECB research shows that the sensitivity of rate expectations to macroeconomic news appears to have increased under the ECB’s current framework guidance regime compared with the period of explicit forward guidance, where short-term rates were mostly constrained by an effective lower bound, implying a smaller information content of surprises for the expected policy path (Chart 8). Markets seem to have incorporated macroeconomic news in rate expectations in a systematic manner only after the explicit formulation of the reaction function criteria, which also came at a time of receding macroeconomic uncertainty. That said, the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive: the economic environment, the degree of uncertainty and the constraints facing monetary policy also changed substantially between those periods. Nevertheless, it highlights how communication frameworks can influence expectations and the transmission of monetary policy.

Finally, incorporating uncertainty into monetary policy communication poses trade-offs.
[
43
]
In view of the high level of external trust in the systematic and comprehensive analysis that underpin the exercise, the information anchor provided by the baseline projections is more valuable than ever in an environment of elevated uncertainty. At the same time, in relation to specific and material risk events, the publication of alternative scenarios can help financial markets, experts and the public understand the possible quantitative impact on inflation and growth dynamics if these alternative scenarios were to materialise.
[
44
]
A communication risk is that excessive focus in placed on the published scenarios rather than also taking into account the comprehensive risk assessment that is contained in each monetary policy statement and expanded upon in the accounts. During any period, a range of risk factors can materialise, such that a wide-angled perspective is needed, rather than taking a reductive approach that overly focuses on any particular set of scenarios.

Conclusions
In this speech, I have outlined some recent ECB research on the science of monetary policy communication. In particular, I have highlighted that new text-based tools, including large language models, allow us to measure central bank communication more systematically, and these confirm that what we say moves financial markets, between meetings as well as on meeting days. Relative to markets-orientated communication, reaching households and firms is more challenging: their attention to inflation rises and falls with inflation itself, which makes clear and consistent communication even more important when inflation is elevated.
In relation to the practice of monetary policy communication, framework guidance is more effective than rate forward guidance when policy rates are away from the effective lower bound. In particular, framework guidance retains the beneficial properties of forward guidance in providing an anchor for rate expectations without incurring the costs in terms of inflexibility and the risk of misperceptions. By communicating a reaction function that spells out the criteria that guide our decisions, our framework guidance has helped markets interpret the incoming data.

SPEECH
Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy
Speech by Isabel Schnabel, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the ECB Conference on Money Markets 2026
Frankfurt am Main, 5 November 2026
The past seven years have been an extraordinary journey.
[
1
]
We have moved from a world in which inflation was persistently too low to one marked by recurrent inflationary shocks; from a historically accommodative monetary policy stance to the fastest tightening cycle in the history of the ECB; and from a deeply integrated global economy to one increasingly shaped by fragmentation and geopolitical tensions.
As I reach the end of my journey here at the ECB, I would like to reflect on the lessons these experiences have taught me about the conduct of monetary policy in a world that has become less predictable.
My remarks today are personal reflections on how the experience of recent years has shaped my thinking about monetary policy and what it may teach us about navigating the challenges ahead.
There are four key takeaways.
Takeaway one: preserve room for manoeuvre by avoiding commitments
The first takeaway is that central banks should prioritise instruments that allow them to adjust monetary policy quickly as conditions change.
We entered the pandemic after a long period in which inflation had been below our target (Slide 2, left-hand side). Globalisation, and the integration of China in particular, had structurally lowered the global cost of producing goods, putting downward pressure on inflation.
At the same time, the global financial crisis and the sovereign debt crisis had weakened public and private balance sheets and left lasting scars on demand, weighing on economic activity and inflation.
Over time, this experience gradually fostered the belief that these forces were permanent, leaving monetary policy primarily focused on bringing inflation back up to target.
As a result, after chronically overpredicting inflation before the pandemic, we were slow to recognise that we had entered a new regime in which we would repeatedly underpredict it (Slide 2, right-hand side).
Indeed, even as evidence of a more substantial and persistent rise in inflation was mounting, the initial reaction was one of relief: the economy finally seemed to be escaping the low-inflation environment.
[
2
]
But the rapid increase in the share of goods and services experiencing inflation above 2% signalled that price pressures were becoming increasingly broad-based (Slide 3).
This exposed two key features of the inflation process that our analytical frameworks had not sufficiently accounted for.
One was the steepening of the Phillips curve, which was in part a result of more frequent price changes as firms sought to protect their profit margins in the face of sharp cost increases (Slide 4).
The other, related feature was the role of firms’ profits in inflation. Unlike the high-inflation period of the 1970s, when inflation was almost entirely driven by growth in unit labour costs, the post-pandemic inflation surge was to a significant extent driven by rising unit profits (Slide 5).
[
3
]
So, the pandemic was a structural break in many of the trends we had witnessed before.
This included a shift in the global balance between savings and investment.
Rising investment needs related to the green and digital transitions, alongside a changing geopolitical environment, have turned the savings glut of the past into a bond glut, as both private and public issuance have increased sharply.
[
4
]
This shift puts upward pressure not only on inflation but also on the natural rate of interest, r* (Slide 6, left-hand side).
[
5
]
None of these shocks or their consequences could have been predicted easily. The lesson is therefore that we should expect the unexpected – and avoid becoming too attached to a particular view of the world or a particular class of models.
This has implications for the design and conduct of monetary policy.
[
6
]
We should be wary of commitments that depend too heavily on a particular economic environment or class of models, leaving little room to adjust when conditions change.
Charles Goodhart – a distinguished scholar of monetary history who has seen the world change more than once – put it this way: “
The world changes, and if the world changes you need sufficient flexibility to change the way that you operate within that
.”
[
7
]
In retrospect, forward guidance during the pandemic was too Odyssean. It tied our hands too closely to a world of persistently low inflation.
The same applies to the choice of other policy instruments.
Some instruments are inherently more agile than others. Policy rates can be adjusted swiftly at each meeting, whereas large-scale asset purchases continue to provide monetary accommodation long after the purchases themselves have ended (Slide 6, right-hand side).
An instrument that is difficult to reverse is itself a form of commitment.
That is also why we emphasise in our monetary policy strategy that our primary monetary policy instrument is the set of key policy rates.
[
8
]
This does not mean that asset purchases are never useful.
[
9
]
They are highly effective in stabilising financial markets that suddenly turn illiquid. And they remain a tool to counter deflationary pressures at the effective lower bound.
One way to preserve flexibility is to separate instruments used to stabilise markets from those used to calibrate the monetary policy stance.
[
10
]
This can limit the scale of asset purchases and make them easier to unwind.
The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) embodies this principle. It provides a dedicated tool to address unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that threaten the transmission of monetary policy, subject to clearly defined criteria.
Takeaway two: what matters is how shocks affect the inflation outlook
The second takeaway is that the appropriate monetary policy response to a shock primarily depends not on its nature, but on its implications for the projected inflation path.
[
11
]
Traditionally, the nature of the shock guided our thinking about how monetary policy should respond to price pressures. The standard prescription was that demand shocks called for an immediate response, while supply shocks could often be looked through, as the shock would either fade on its own or weaker growth would dampen emerging price pressures, reducing the need for monetary tightening.
This distinction can be misleading, for two reasons.
First, central banks rarely face one shock at a time. During the pandemic, supply chain disruptions, pent-up demand and unprecedented fiscal and monetary policy support interacted in ways that were difficult to disentangle (Slide 7, left-hand side).
[
12
]
Russia’s unjustified invasion of Ukraine added a major energy and food price shock to an already challenging environment. Such overlapping shocks can prolong the period of elevated inflation and make the “last mile” of disinflation particularly challenging.
[
13
]
Services inflation was still running above 3% before the start of the conflict in the Middle East, reflecting the drawn-out adjustment to the earlier inflation surge, including through staggered wage negotiations (Slide 7, right-hand side).
Today, we again face overlapping shocks, from geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices to the rapid expansion of AI-related investment and large fiscal spending needs, including for defence. These developments affect demand, productive capacity, prices and financial conditions through different channels and over different horizons.
Second, a sufficiently large and persistent adverse supply shock can push projected inflation above target, requiring a timely monetary policy response. What begins as a relative price adjustment can turn into a broader inflation problem through indirect price effects, wage dynamics and changes in inflation expectations.
This is why we are closely monitoring these developments. In response to the latest energy shock, consumer inflation expectations over the medium to longer term have increased and gradually moved away from our 2% target (Slide 8).
The lesson is therefore that monetary policy cannot be calibrated on the basis of simple classifications of shocks. What matters is how shocks affect the inflation outlook.
This matters even more in a world in which adverse supply-side shocks are likely to become more frequent and persistent owing to geopolitical fragmentation and climate change.
[
14
]
The role of climate change for monetary policy has long been a source of contention. But the evidence is increasingly clear. More frequent floods, heatwaves and droughts lower agricultural yields, disrupt supply and damage infrastructure, all of which feed into price dynamics (Slide 9).
[
15
]
And “climateflation” is just one way in which climate change is becoming a challenge for price stability, bringing it squarely within our primary mandate.
[
16
]
So, for each shock, we need to assess its size and persistence, the state of the economy and the risk of inflation becoming entrenched in expectations and in price and wage-setting.
The ECB’s response to the conflict in the Middle East reflects these lessons.
ECB staff rapidly developed projection scenarios with varying assumptions about the indirect and second-round effects of the energy shock. Monetary policy, in turn, responded to the expected persistence of these inflationary pressures in a timely and forward-looking manner.
As a result, we are now well positioned to address the current inflation challenge.
Takeaway three: protect monetary dominance
The third takeaway is that the ECB’s ability to fulfil its primary mandate relies on robust fiscal and regulatory frameworks that ensure monetary dominance.
During the post-pandemic inflation surge, the ECB demonstrated its ability to tighten monetary policy forcefully, even though higher interest rates could have pushed the economy into recession or posed risks to fiscal and financial stability.
The resilience of the banking sector was an essential condition for monetary policy to act as needed to restore price stability. This was largely thanks to the financial reforms introduced in the wake of the global financial crisis. Strong capital positions and healthy profitability allowed banks to absorb the rise in interest rates without coming under financial strain (Slide 10).
Structural changes threaten monetary dominance
Two developments, if left unchecked, could threaten monetary dominance in the future: first, structural changes in the financial sector, including the rise of non-bank finance; and second, the increase in public debt.
[
17
]
Over the past two decades, partly in response to tighter bank regulation, there has been a massive shift in the provision of financial services away from banks to non-bank financial intermediaries. Non-banks now hold financial assets on a par with those held by banks (Slide 11, left-hand side).
[
18
]
At the same time, euro area public debt as a share of GDP has increased by nearly 20 percentage points since the early 2000s, with large heterogeneity across member countries (Slide 11, right-hand side). This rise in part reflects the successive crises we have faced.
Rising public debt is a global trend across advanced economies. The IMF projects government debt in the United States to rise to 145% of GDP in 2031, up from 124% last year. For China, it projects an increase to 122% over the same period, up from 99%.
These two shifts interact in important ways.
As central banks reduce the asset portfolios accumulated during years of monetary accommodation, a greater share of government debt must be absorbed by price-sensitive private investors.
Hedge funds in particular are holding an increasing share of sovereign debt, often financed through repos, and they now play a key role in intermediating sovereign bond markets (Slide 12, left-hand side).
As a result, monetary policy is transmitted more rapidly.
[
19
]
When policy tightens, higher interest rates will feed quickly into government financing costs through the higher funding costs of non-bank lenders. This dynamic is reinforced by governments shifting towards shorter debt maturities (Slide 12, right-hand side).
At higher levels of public debt, however, non-linear effects are more likely to emerge.
When volatility rises, falling collateral values, higher margin requirements or reduced access to funding can force leveraged investors to unwind their positions. The “dash for cash” episode in 2020 and the liability-driven investment (LDI) crisis in the United Kingdom in 2022 illustrated how such dynamics can destabilise sovereign bond markets, the bedrock of our financial system.
To restore transmission, central banks may then be forced to stabilise markets to prevent a liquidity crisis from turning into a full-blown credit crisis, which would likely also spill over to the banking sector.
[
20
]
Such interventions can interfere with the central bank’s mandate and threaten monetary dominance.
There are two lessons to be learned from this.
Proper regulation reduces the risk of financial dominance
First, a sound financial system reduces the risk of financial dominance.
For this reason, governments should resist the current push towards deregulating the banking sector.
[
21
]
Many of the arguments put forward in favour of deregulation are flawed. Its benefits are doubtful and its potential costs are significant.
Thanks to the reforms implemented following the global financial crisis, the banking system was an anchor of stability during recent shocks.
Yet the shift of financial activity towards the less regulated non-bank sector has made the financial system more fragile. It also creates risks for banking sector stability: banks are closely interconnected with non-banks and increasingly rely on them as a source of funding, creating channels through which stress can spread across the financial system (Slide 13).
Leverage, reliance on short-term funding and interconnectedness in core markets therefore require stronger oversight and a more effective macroprudential framework. Stronger regulation of non-banks would also bolster the case for considering their access to central bank facilities, which could further support systemic stability.
Consolidation and growth reduce the risk of fiscal dominance
Second, prudent fiscal policy reduces the risk of fiscal dominance.
In the changed interest rate environment, it has become more difficult to put public finances back on a sustainable path. This challenge is well illustrated by the evolution of the differential between the effective interest rate paid on debt,
r
, and the economy’s growth rate,
g
.
For years,
r-g
was negative (Slide 14, left-hand side). Such an environment allows governments to bring debt ratios down, even when running primary deficits. But the differential has now turned positive in many countries and is likely to rise further as governments refinance maturing debt at today’s higher interest rates.
At the same time, potential growth in the euro area has been on a declining trend and is expected to weaken further (Slide 14, right-hand side). Population ageing is weighing on labour supply, while investment and productivity growth are unlikely to be strong enough to offset the resulting drag on potential growth.
Efforts are therefore needed on both sides of the
r-g
differential.
On the
r
side, a credible fiscal path helps contain both risk premia and interest rate expenditure. The best contribution the ECB can make is to keep the inflation risk premium low by ensuring that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored (Slide 15, left-hand side).
On the
g
side, the euro area needs to regain competitiveness.
[
22
]
For a long time, productivity growth in the euro area has been weaker than in the United States (Slide 15, right-hand side).
Achieving a lasting improvement requires progress on two fronts: strengthening Europe’s capacity to innovate and enabling the diffusion of new technologies across the economy.
Both depend on scale.
Boosting innovation requires an environment that allows promising ideas to grow into successful businesses on a European scale.
Yet fragmented capital markets make it harder for firms to secure financing as they grow, while fragmented product markets limit the potential returns for investors. These obstacles reinforce each other: investors hesitate to finance companies that cannot scale up, while companies struggle to scale up without access to sufficient capital.
The Single Market is critical to breaking this cycle. A product that can be sold across a market of more than 450 million Europeans offers a much greater growth opportunity than one that can be sold only in one country.
Yet, despite decades of integration, barriers within the Single Market remain substantial. ECB estimates suggest that internal barriers are equivalent to tariffs of 96% for services and 67% for goods (Slide 16).
A powerful step towards overcoming this fragmentation is a 28th regime: a unified European corporate framework that lowers barriers to cross-border activity, makes it easier to raise capital and attract talent, and allows innovative companies to scale up more quickly across the European Union.
[
23
]
The proposal currently under discussion could be an important step in that direction. A watered-down version, by contrast, would risk becoming another lost opportunity.
But innovation alone is not enough.
Productivity also depends on how effectively existing and new technologies are adopted throughout the economy. Here, too, scale matters. Smaller firms tend to be less productive, partly because they lack the resources to cover the fixed costs of adopting new technologies (Slide 17, left-hand side).
This is particularly urgent as AI opens up new possibilities to transform production and raise productivity (Slide 17, right-hand side). Europe cannot afford to repeat the experience of the digital revolution of the 1990s and 2000s, when it was slow to adopt and exploit new technologies at scale.
[
24
]
The ECB is playing its part by introducing the digital euro and by harnessing distributed ledger technology (DLT) and tokenisation to future-proof Europe’s wholesale financial markets, reduce fragmentation and modernise the implementation of monetary policy.
[
25
]
These efforts will support strategic autonomy and help safeguard Europe against excessive reliance on foreign currency-denominated stablecoins, which could undermine monetary sovereignty and create risks for financial stability.
[
26
]
Takeaway four: implement monetary policy efficiently
The fourth takeaway is that monetary policy should be implemented efficiently with a balance sheet that is no larger than necessary.
In the wake of the global financial crisis, many central banks moved towards operating with abundant reserves. They did so not because this was necessarily their preferred way of implementing monetary policy, but as a consequence of large-scale asset purchases.
By buying assets on a massive scale, central banks injected far more reserves into the system than banks needed to satisfy their liquidity demands.
This came at a cost. Private market activity was displaced, asset prices were distorted and central banks, and thus ultimately taxpayers, were exposed to financial risks.
[
27
]
At one point, the scarcity of safe assets in the euro area was so acute that rates on some specialised repo transactions traded at a premium of more than 50 basis points above the ECB’s deposit facility rate (Slide 18, left-hand side).
Abundant reserves also changed the liability structure of bank balance sheets.
As reserves were injected into the system, banks issued more short-term, uninsured deposits. But these claims on liquidity did not decline in step with reserves when central banks subsequently reduced their balance sheets (Slide 18, right-hand side).
[
28
]
This created a ratchet effect. Banks became more dependent on central bank liquidity, potentially making the system more vulnerable in periods of stress. This experience highlights the limits of the Friedman rule in practice: supplying reserves abundantly is not without costs.
There are two lessons from this.
The first is that, as part of quantitative normalisation, we are winding down the portfolios accumulated under the asset purchase programme (APP) and the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP). The monetary policy motivation for these portfolios no longer exists.
In principle, we can reduce them all the way to zero, unless we were to return to the effective lower bound, in which case renewed purchases might become necessary to protect price stability.
The second lesson is that banks are best placed to assess their own liquidity needs. The central bank should ensure that these needs can be met on appropriate terms, while encouraging banks to tap private funding markets before accessing central bank facilities.
The ECB’s new operational framework reflects this insight.
[
29
]
Every week banks can request as much liquidity as they need through our standard refinancing operations at a fixed rate and against a broad set of collateral.
As excess liquidity continues to decline, we expect banks to make increasing use of these operations. Accessing central bank refinancing operations will again become a normal part of banks’ liquidity management, without any stigma attached to it.
[
30
]
The recent standard refinancing operations covering the month and year-end were encouraging. They attracted significant demand from a broad set of banks.
Over time, the take-up of our standard refinancing operations will give us valuable information about banks’ demand for reserves.
In particular, if the amounts requested continue to rise and remain elevated, this will indicate that an increasing share of banks’ borrowing reflects persistent liquidity needs rather than temporary fluctuations.
At that point, it would make sense to meet the more stable part of this demand through structural operations rather than requiring banks to roll over large amounts every week.
Complementing our regular operations with structural liquidity-providing instruments, including longer-term refinancing operations and a structural securities portfolio, will provide banks with a more stable source of liquidity.
In my reading, the current structure of the ECB’s balance sheet implies the following sequence in this transition.
[
31
]
As the sizeable legacy APP and PEPP portfolios will continue to provide liquidity for a long time, it is natural to begin by introducing structural longer-term refinancing operations. In addition, the Eurosystem holds assets for non-monetary policy purposes, which also contribute to the supply of reserves.
Once the legacy portfolios have run off sufficiently, a structural securities portfolio will gradually be built.
So, liquidity demand will ultimately be satisfied through a mix of instruments, also reflecting that part of bank’s liquidity needs is driven by autonomous factors beyond their control. But the fundamental principle will remain unchanged: the marginal unit of liquidity will be supplied through our standard refinancing operations in response to banks’ demand, rather than being injected at the central bank’s initiative.
The advantage is that we do not need to estimate banks’ liquidity needs in advance or maintain an additional buffer in the face of uncertainty about the amount of liquidity the system requires.
If calibrated appropriately, such a framework can achieve the best of both worlds: efficiently implementing monetary policy with fewer side effects, while ensuring that banks have the liquidity they need.
Conclusion
Let me conclude by bringing together the four takeaways from these reflections.
First, preserving room for manoeuvre allows monetary policy to respond quickly when circumstances change in unexpected ways.
Second, monetary policy should respond to the implications of shocks for the inflation outlook, not to their nature.
Third, safeguarding monetary dominance allows central banks to act decisively when price stability is at risk.
And finally, implementing monetary policy efficiently with a balance sheet that is no larger than necessary reduces side effects, preserves future policy space and fosters market activity.
These four takeaways reflect what the past seven years have taught me about conducting monetary policy in a volatile world.
The economic environment will keep changing. But the experience built over recent years leaves the ECB well equipped to navigate any stormy waters ahead, while remaining firmly focused on what ultimately matters: price stability.
Thank you very much.
